t: 6 Critical First-Week-Of-School Strategies For Difficult Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2019/07/27/first-week-of-school-strategies-difficult-students/
q: Focusing on difficult students, checking in on them, using proximity with them, and otherwise spending more time with them than your other students are all forms of labeling.
When you treat challenging students like everyone else, they tend to behave like everyone else.
Difficult students have been praised so often and for so long that it’s lost all its meaning.
Never tiptoe around difficult students or be fearful of holding them accountable. These, too, are labeling behaviors that can also give them a sense of entitlement.
You can build strong rapport with difficult students by just allowing them to enjoy being a regular student.
In most cases, difficult students don’t need a counselor. They need a leader and role model who sees their worth and potential and treats them as if they really can do it.

t: My Number One Goal On The First Day Of School
q: My number one goal on the first day of school is that my students love being in my class.
You trigger the Law of Reciprocity, which causes them to want to repay you for creating a classroom they’re happy to be part of.
Emphasize that your classroom management plan is for them , not you, and it’s sole purpose is to protect their right to learn and enjoy school without being bothered, bullied, or interrupted.
Teach at least one routine—like entering the classroom or lining up for lunch—with the same energy and commitment you would the xy-graph, the scientific method, or the very fundamentals of grammar.
Children as young as five recognize great teaching when they see it, and they’re changed by it.
It’s common to confuse rules with encouragements—which are behaviors you’d like to see in your students but are ultimately unenforceable.
Do your best. Be ready to learn. Try new things. Have fun. Dream big. Make wise choices.
Rules protect your freedom to teach and your students’ right to learn and enjoy school. That’s it.
Encouragements like those listed above, on the other hand, do no such thing and are all but impossible to enforce.
They’re also incredibly confusing to students—and hurtful if you do attempt to enforce them.
Some readers even discovered that none of their rules covered actual disruptions.
